A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IQT and ConformalDAgger research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original time-series experiments, simulated robot-learning experiments, and physical robot sponging results, including supplementary results in its appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds threshold sensitivity experiments, environment-shift evaluations, and Robosuite nut-assembly results.

M1.justification: The IQT update, intermittent ACI extension, and ConformalDAgger procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 explicitly includes query-probability computation already described in v1 and combines the upper/lower update notation; these are explanatory changes.

E1.justification: v2 adds environment shift through a changed robot starting position to the reaching experiments. Appendix G also introduces Robosuite nut assembly under unchanged and relocated-peg conditions. The original time-series datasets and sponging task remain.

E2.justification: The reaching and hardware comparisons expand from EnsembleDAgger alone to EnsembleDAgger, LazyDAgger, and SafeDAgger. The added methods also participate in the supplementary feedback-frequency comparisons; their inclusion is confirmed by the result figures.

E3.justification: The simulation uncertainty threshold changes from 0.09 to 0.06. Section 6 changes hardware demonstrations from 100 to 50, interactive executions from 50 to 25, initial/fine-tuning iterations from 60K/60K to 50K/35K, and buffer capacity from 12K to 6K. Hardware reporting switches to robot-requested interventions. Nut assembly introduces autonomous success over 50 rollouts and action counts restricted to successful episodes.

E4.justification: New Appendix B examines threshold sensitivity across all four robotic methods, including failure at excessively high ConformalDAgger thresholds. Environment-shift tests add robustness evidence, and existing feedback-frequency analyses expand to additional comparators and scenarios. The original expert-shift case study is retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Figure 5 reports standard errors across five seeds in v2 rather than ten in v1. The new threshold analysis reports averaging over three seeds. Time-series reporting remains based on five seeds with the same uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: v2 updates robotic result curves and adds comparator, sensitivity, environment-shift, and nut-assembly findings, while Tables 1–9 retain identical numerical values. Hardware Figure 6 changes from about 100 human-intervention timesteps under expert shift to about 35 robot-requested timesteps; the changed metric and experimental settings prevent treating this as a direct performance improvement.

T1.justification: Appendix F newly states an expert-realizability assumption for the imitation-learning setting. The IQT and IACI propositions, bounds, and proofs otherwise remain unchanged, moving from v1 Appendices A–B to v2 Appendices C–D.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions: intermittent conformal calibration, asymptotic coverage guarantees, and uncertainty-guided feedback that supports adaptation to expert shift. The conclusion preserves these claims; additional experiments primarily supply supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of high-threshold failure, reliance on human-gated feedback, and finite-horizon coverage limitations. It explains LazyDAgger's hardware behavior through inconsistent querying across episodes. The original caveat about difficulties retaining DAgger performance guarantees is replaced by discussion of expert realizability, changing the stated limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds hardware safety-classifier inputs and threshold-selection details, plus nut-assembly state/action descriptions and an access link for 30 demonstrations containing 2,687 state-action pairs. Much existing implementation information is retained. However, Appendix H.1 still specifies 60K initial training iterations, conflicting with Section 6's revised 50K.

R1.justification: v2 adds Spencer et al. (2021) when discussing covariate shift and realizability, while removing the separate nonstationary-expert discussion and several associated citations. The robotics conformal-prediction discussion moves to Appendix A rather than being removed. The central research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: v2 compresses related work and several method paragraphs, streamlines Algorithm 1, revises experimental discussion, and reorganizes the appendices. Most introductory and methodological wording remains intact. The publication header changes from 'Under review' to the ICLR 2025 conference designation.

P2.justification: Figures 5 and 6 are substantially redesigned for additional comparators, scenarios, and revised hardware reporting. Supplementary simulation plots gain comparator curves and environment-shift rows. New Figures 7 and 13 present threshold sensitivity and nut-assembly results, while retained tables and illustrations are redistributed.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by addressing v1's reliance on one robotic comparator and lack of threshold-sensitivity checks. Additional baselines, explicit threshold comparisons, and environment-shift and nut-assembly evaluations make the intervention-versus-adaptation findings more convincing. Fewer reported simulation seeds and the unresolved 50K/60K training-budget inconsistency are drawbacks, but do not outweigh these gains.
